cases.issue_title: Transform dialog resizes continually as typing
cases.issue_body:
This is a relatively recent regression, but I don't know, off the top of my head, what the likely cause is. 

### To Reproduce
Steps to reproduce the behavior:
1. Use Edit Cells... -> Transform to bring up the dialog
2. Start typing a GREL expression

### Current Results

The Transform popup dialog continually resizes as you're typing GREL expressions, driven by the appearance and disappearance of the syntax error messages as one types partially formed expressions. This is SUPER annoying and distracting.

The dialog also resizes when different tabs are selected, which is undesirable.

### Expected Behavior

UI stays stable as the user types.

### Additional context and analysis (from comment below)

This regression was introduced by https://github.com/OpenRefine/OpenRefine/pull/7429 which was attempting to fix https://github.com/OpenRefine/OpenRefine/issues/7202, so we should double check that that bug stays fixed. Also relevant is https://github.com/OpenRefine/OpenRefine/pull/3587 which was targeted to fix https://github.com/OpenRefine/OpenRefine/issues/3565.

I think we may want to go back to before all this and rethink how the layout is done. I think adjusting the size of the dialog based on its contents is distracting, so we may want to keep it fixed or a fixed percentage of the viewport size.

Some thoughts on requirements (let's refine/confirm these before attempting an implementation):

- Selecting different tabs shouldn't change the size of the dialog as currently happens
- OK & Cancel buttons should always be visible
- Inner components shouldn't overflow boundaries of containing elements
- Text on Help tab should get wrapped to fit available width
- Expressions (History & Starred tabs) should use horizontal scroll bar if needed (BUT only if needed. Right now it always seems to be present even when not really needed)
- Preview tab should use horizontal scroll bar (and/or wrap?) to handle long preview values
- the user should be able to manually resize the dialog to their preferred size
- the default dialog size should be larger, similar to what it used to be

cases.issue_title: Wikibase : Don't show "required statement" constraints for edits on existing entities
cases.issue_body:
When editing existing Wikibase entities, OpenRefine displays false positive QA scrutinizer warnings (such as "required statement" constraints from `ItemRequiresScrutinizer`). Because OpenRefine's local schema preview does not query online entity statements, it assumes required properties are missing on the target entity, confusing users during schema building and upload preview.

### To Reproduce
Steps to reproduce the behavior:
1. Open an OpenRefine project with cells reconciled to existing Wikibase/Wikidata entities (e.g., Katowice `Q588`).
2. Go to **Extensions** > **Wikibase** > **Edit Wikibase schema**.
3. Add a statement to an existing entity using a property that has an "item requires statement" constraint (e.g., `male population (P1540)`, which requires `country (P17)`).
4. Click on the **Issues** tab in the schema preview dialog.

### Current Results
OpenRefine displays a Quality Assurance warning:
**male population (P1540) requires statement with property P17.**
 *This property is expected to have another statement with property P17 such as on item Katowice (Q588). If the item already has statements with property P17 in Wikidata, then this warning can be ignored.*

### Expected Behavior
OpenRefine should not generate "required statement" constraint warnings for edits on existing entities, as local schema preview cannot check existing online statements and the resulting warning is a false positive that misleads users.

### Versions
-Operating System: Windows 11 Version 25H2 (Build 26200.8894)
-Browser Version: 151.0.7922.71 (Official Build) (64-bit)
-JRE or JDK Version: JDK 21+
-OpenRefine: 3.10-SNAPSHOT (master)

### Additional context
Reported after an OpenRefine-Wikidata training session at Wikimania, where trainers and participants were misled by false constraint warnings when editing existing Wikidata items.

cases.issue_title: [Feature Request]: secrets_filter: keep HashiCorp Nomad/Consul tokens and literal credential assignments out of history
cases.issue_body:
### Problem

`secrets_filter` keeps a command out of history when it matches a known secret format. HashiCorp Nomad and Consul ACL tokens have no format of their own. They are bare UUIDs, so no format pattern can match them. They reach the command line in a small set of fixed forms:

```sh
export NOMAD_TOKEN=00000000-0000-0000-0000-000000000000
CONSUL_HTTP_TOKEN=00000000-0000-0000-0000-000000000000 consul members
nomad job status -token=00000000-0000-0000-0000-000000000000
curl -H "X-Nomad-Token: 00000000-0000-0000-0000-000000000000" http://127.0.0.1:4646/v1/jobs
curl -H "X-Consul-Token: 00000000-0000-0000-0000-000000000000" http://127.0.0.1:8500/v1/agent/members
curl -H "X-Vault-Token: $(cat token)" ...   # and with a literal hvs. or legacy s. token
```

In 18.17.1 none of these are filtered, and neither is `VAULT_TOKEN=hvs.…`. The history then holds a live cluster credential, and with sync on, every machine of that user holds it too.

### What has landed already

#4364 adds a `HashiCorp Vault token` format (`hvs.`/`hvb.`) and a `Credential variable` rule that matches `NOMAD_TOKEN=…` and `CONSUL_HTTP_TOKEN=…`. That is a big step, thank you. As far as I can read `crates/atuin-common/src/secrets/structural.rs`, the named and structural rules only redact. They do not decide what `secrets_filter` keeps. So on `main` a `NOMAD_TOKEN=<uuid>` command is still saved to history, and so are the `-token=` and `X-*-Token` header forms.

### Request

One of these, in order of preference:

1. Let `secrets_filter` also drop commands that match a credential assignment where the value is a literal (not `$VAR` or `$(…)`). An opt-in setting is fine if the false-positive risk is too high for a default.
2. Or add targeted filter patterns for the HashiCorp forms above: `NOMAD_TOKEN`, `CONSUL_HTTP_TOKEN` and `VAULT_TOKEN` assignments, `-token=` on the `nomad`, `consul` and `vault` CLIs, and the `X-Nomad-Token`, `X-Consul-Token` and `X-Vault-Token` headers, each with a literal value.

I am happy to open a PR for option 2 if that is the preferred direction.

cases.issue_title: [Bug]: Zsh integration removes WezTerm's OSC 133 input marker when the PTY proxy is inactive
cases.issue_body:
### What did you expect to happen?

I use WezTerm's Zsh shell integration, which marks prompts, command input, and command output with OSC 133 semantic zones.

When Atuin's PTY proxy does not own the current terminal, I expected Atuin to leave OSC 133 markers from another shell integration unchanged. In particular, WezTerm's `OSC 133;B` marker should remain in `PROMPT` so that entered commands are classified as `Input` zones.

### What happened?

After updating Atuin from 18.15.2 to 18.19.0, WezTerm stopped detecting `Input` semantic zones. Output zones still work. I checked the Zsh integration in 18.20.0, 18.20.1, 18.21.0, 18.22.0, and the current `main` branch; the same marker removal is still present.

Atuin's generated Zsh integration runs `_atuin_precmd` after WezTerm's `__wezterm_semantic_precmd`. `_atuin_precmd` calls `__atuin_osc133_wrap_prompt`, which removes `OSC 133;A` and `OSC 133;B` from `PROMPT` and `RPROMPT`:

```zsh
__atuin_prompt="${__atuin_prompt//$__atuin_osc133_prompt_start/}"
__atuin_prompt="${__atuin_prompt//$__atuin_osc133_prompt_end/}"
__atuin_rprompt="${__atuin_rprompt//$__atuin_osc133_prompt_start/}"
__atuin_rprompt="${__atuin_rprompt//$__atuin_osc133_prompt_end/}"
```

In Atuin 18.22.0, the markers are added back only when Atuin determines that its PTY proxy owns the current terminal:

```zsh
if [[ "${__atuin_pty_proxy_owns_tty:-0}" = 1 ]]; then
    PROMPT="${__atuin_osc133_prompt_start}${__atuin_prompt}"
    RPROMPT="${__atuin_rprompt}${__atuin_osc133_prompt_end}"
else
    [[ "$__atuin_orig_prompt" == "$__atuin_prompt" ]] || PROMPT="$__atuin_prompt"
    [[ "$__atuin_orig_rprompt" == "$__atuin_rprompt" ]] || RPROMPT="$__atuin_rprompt"
fi
```

Without an active Atuin PTY proxy, `__atuin_pty_proxy_owns_tty` is `0`. Since removing WezTerm's marker changes the prompt, the `else` branch writes the stripped prompt back to `PROMPT`.

The 18.22.0 change from #4079, "Make PTY proxy aware of other PTYs," does not fix this case. That change detects whether Atuin is directly attached to its own proxy rather than running through another PTY such as tmux or screen. It changes how the active proxy is detected, but the prompt wrapper still removes markers when the proxy is inactive.

My `precmd` hook order is:

```text
prompt_starship_precmd
__wezterm_semantic_precmd
__wezterm_user_vars_precmd
__wezterm_osc7
_atuin_precmd
```

Because `_atuin_precmd` runs after WezTerm's hook, the final prompt no longer contains `OSC 133;B`. WezTerm then classifies the entered command as part of the `Prompt` zone:

```text
type=Prompt text="<rendered prompt>\nprint -r -- wezterm-zone-test"
input=0
output=2
```

Before Atuin removes the marker, or with the workaround below, the command is classified correctly:

```text
type=Prompt text="<rendered prompt>"
type=Input text="print -r -- wezterm-zone-test"
type=Output text="wezterm-zone-test"
input=1
```

### Steps to reproduce

1. Enable WezTerm's Zsh shell integration.
2. Enable Atuin's Zsh integration.
3. Leave Atuin's PTY proxy disabled or otherwise inactive.
4. Start a new Zsh session in WezTerm.
5. Run a command.
6. Inspect the zones with this WezTerm Lua callback:

```lua
wezterm.action_callback(function(_, pane)
    wezterm.log_info("input zones: " .. #pane:get_semantic_zones("Input"))
end)
```

The result is `input zones: 0`.

The prompt mutation can also be seen by inspecting `PROMPT` before and after `_atuin_precmd` runs.

### Workaround

Re-emitting `OSC 133;B` from `zle-line-init` restores the input zones:

```zsh
if [[ "${TERM_PROGRAM-}" == "WezTerm" ]]; then
    autoload -Uz add-zle-hook-widget

    _wezterm_mark_input_zone() {
        printf '\e]133;B\a'
    }

    add-zle-hook-widget line-init _wezterm_mark_input_zone
fi
```

### Possible fix

When Atuin's PTY proxy does not own the current terminal, the prompt wrapper should avoid removing OSC 133 markers emitted by another shell integration.

### Environment

- Reproduced with Atuin 18.19.0; confirmed in the generated Zsh integration through 18.22.0 and current `main`
- Shell: Zsh 5.9.2
- Terminal: WezTerm
- OS: macOS
- `ATUIN_PTY_PROXY_ACTIVE`: unset

cases.issue_title: Bring back basic HTTP access/sync logs in Docker (or update RUST_LOG documentation)
cases.issue_body:
#### Context & Problem
Since version 18.20.0 (specifically after the migration to the tracing framework and OTel), the standard HTTP access logs (like POST /sync) no longer appear in the Docker container logs.

When trying to enable them using the RUST_LOG=info,atuin_server=debug environment variable (as often seen in community compose files and docs), the server simply outputs a warning and ignores the debug directive:

```bash 
warning: some trace filter directives would enable traces that are disabled statically
 | `atuin_server=debug` would enable the DEBUG level for the `atuin_server` target
 = note: the static max level is `info`
 = help: to enable DEBUG logging, remove the `max_level_info` feature from the `tracing` crate
```
Because the official Docker image is compiled with the max_level_info feature enabled, tower_http access logs (which seem to default to debug/trace) are completely stripped out.

Why this matters
For users self-hosting Atuin via Docker, these basic access logs are crucial. They are used to:

Verify if reverse proxies (Nginx, Traefik, Caddy) are correctly forwarding requests to the container.

Monitor general server health and active client syncs.

Feed logs to security tools like Fail2Ban.

#### Proposed Solutions
I would like to suggest one of the following approaches to improve this experience:

Log HTTP requests at the INFO level: Change the tower_http configuration so that basic request logs (like syncs and registrations) are treated as INFO rather than DEBUG. This would restore the basic observability that self-hosters rely on without needing debug flags.

Provide a way to enable DEBUG in Docker: Remove the max_level_info static restriction from the official Docker builds, allowing users to opt-in to DEBUG logs via the RUST_LOG environment variable if they need to troubleshoot.
OR:
Update the Documentation: If restoring these logs is not aligned with the project's current goals (e.g., due to performance reasons), sugest consider updating the Docker compose examples and documentation to remove RUST_LOG=info,atuin_server=debug. Currently, it leads users to a dead end and generates startup warnings.

cases.issue_title: Accordion: backend `open=True` doesn't visually expand on an already-rendered accordion; first header click is consumed (regression vs 5.x)

### Describe the bug

reviving the closed issue #12846 and #12843

After upgrading from 5.49.1 to 6.28.0, returning gr.Accordion(open=True) from an event handler updates the component's logical open state but does not visually expand the accordion if the component was already rendered on the page.
Consequences:
An accordion that should be expanded renders collapsed.
The first click on its header appears to do nothing (the internal state was already flipped to true by the backend payload, so the first click toggles it back to false with no visible change). Only the second click actually expands it.
The open state itself is handled correctly server-side — it is only the frontend visual state that desynchronizes.
This worked correctly in 5.49.1: the same code expands the accordion immediately and a single click is enough to collapse/expand afterwards.

### Have you searched existing issues?  🔎

- [x] I have searched and found no existing issues

### Reproduction

```python
import gradio as gr

PAGE_SIZE = 16
NUM_PAGES = 4
TOTAL     = PAGE_SIZE * NUM_PAGES          # 64 blocks

# Saved session data: slot #2 of every page is expanded (blocks 2, 18, 34, 50)
```

cases.issue_title: gr.Workflow: cache node outputs so re-running reuses unchanged upstream results instead of re-executing the whole subgraph
cases.issue_body:
### Problem

Currently, running any node on a `gr.Workflow` canvas re-executes its entire upstream subgraph.

This can get very expensive when upstream nodes involve inference APIs, GPU workloads, or other slow operations. Even when none of the upstream inputs have changed, those nodes are executed again.

Some form of caching or memoization of node outputs across runs would make `gr.Workflow` much more practical for iterative workflows.

### Expected behavior

If a node and its inputs have not changed, its previous output should be reusable when executing a downstream node.

For example, if the graph looks like:

`Generate Image → Edit Image`

and the generated image already exists, re-running `Edit Image` should not necessarily cause `Generate Image` to execute again.

My understanding is that ComfyUI behaves similarly: you can re-run a node and its descendants multiple times without re-executing unchanged upstream nodes. `gr.Workflow` currently has no equivalent.

### Example

In the attached demo example, I am trying to iterate on the downstream image-editing node. Notice that every time I run it, the entire upstream graph runs again, causing the source image to be regenerated before it can be edited. You can access this app here as well: https://huggingface.co/spaces/ysharma/gr-workflow-klein-studio

https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/57ca0209-f8ae-4045-aa72-4dac51416c3e

Having cached/memoized outputs for unchanged upstream nodes would make this kind of iterative workflow significantly faster and cheaper.

cases.issue_body:
### Describe the bug

A formula that contains `<` is not rendered by `gr.Markdown` or `gr.Chatbot`. The output is cut off at the `<`, and everything after it in the same paragraph disappears too, including other formulas. `>` works fine.

For `Bounds: $$a<b$$ and $$c>d$$ hold.`, only `Bounds: $$a` is shown.

This was reported before in #10112, which was closed after the reporter worked around it by writing `<`.

`MarkdownCode.svelte` takes the LaTeX blocks out before running marked (added in #8822 so that marked does not mangle the LaTeX) and puts them back into marked's HTML output unchanged. A `<` inside a block therefore ends up in the HTML unescaped, and the browser reads `<b$$ and $$c>` as the start of an unknown element, which the sanitizer then removes together with its content. Before #8822, marked escaped the `<` itself.

Escaping each block when it is put back should fix this. KaTeX auto-render reads the DOM text nodes, so `<` is still seen as `<` and the formula renders. I plan to open a PR for this.

cases.issue_title: gr.Audio(streaming=True): microphone stays open after the recording is stopped
cases.issue_body:
**Describe the bug**

With a streaming microphone `gr.Audio`, pressing Stop ends the recording but leaves a microphone `MediaStream` live, so the browser keeps the microphone open until the page is closed.

In `js/audio/interactive/InteractiveAudio.svelte`, `prepare_audio()` opens a stream with `navigator.mediaDevices.getUserMedia({ audio: true })` and hands it to the streaming `MediaRecorder`. `stop()` (and the `onDestroy` handler) only call `recorder.stop()`. Stopping a `MediaRecorder` does not stop the tracks of the stream it records, and no reference to the stream is kept, so its tracks are never stopped.

Only one stream stays open: later recordings reuse the same recorder (`inited`), so it does not accumulate. The waveform visualizer's own stream (`StreamAudio.svelte`, `waveformRecord?.startMic()` / `stopMic()`) is closed correctly.

**Reproduction**

```python
import gradio as gr

with gr.Blocks() as demo:
    a = gr.Audio(sources=["microphone"], type="numpy", streaming=True)
    o = gr.Textbox()
    a.stream(lambda x: str(None if x is None else len(x[1])), a, o)

demo.launch()
```

1. Click Record, allow the microphone, record a couple of seconds, click Stop.
2. The mic stays in use. To confirm from DevTools, wrap `navigator.mediaDevices.getUserMedia` before recording, keep the returned streams, and check `stream.getTracks().map(t => t.readyState)` after Stop: one stream still reports `"live"` after each recording.

**Suggested fix**

Keep a reference to the stream created in `prepare_audio()`, stop its tracks in `stop()` and in `onDestroy` (`stream.getTracks().forEach(t => t.stop())`), and reset `inited = false` so the next recording opens a fresh stream.

**System info**

gradio 6.28.0 (same code on `main`), Windows 10, Chromium 138-based browser (fake media device used for the measurement).

Found with AI assistance (Claude Code) on my machine.

cases.issue_title: convert_to_16_bit_audio performs scaling in narrow dtypes, causing overflow
cases.issue_body:
### Describe the bug

## Problem

8-bit PCM scaling happens before widening the array. With NumPy 2.3.5, multipliers 256/257 are out of bounds for int8/uint8, so conversion raises OverflowError. Float16 scaling also rounds 32767 to 32768, flipping the positive endpoint when cast to int16.

## Reproduction

```python
import numpy as np
from gradio.processing_utils import convert_to_16_bit_audio
for dtype, values in [(np.int8, [-128, 0, 127]), (np.uint8, [0, 128, 255]), (np.float16, [-1, 0, 1])]:
    try:
        print(dtype, convert_to_16_bit_audio(np.array(values, dtype=dtype)))
    except Exception as e:
        print(dtype, type(e).__name__, str(e))
```

Expected int16 outputs: int8 -> [-32768, 0, 32512]; uint8 -> [-32768, 128, 32767] under the existing mapping; float16 -> [-32767, 0, 32767].

Widen int8 to int16 before multiplying by 256; widen uint8 to int32 before `* 257 - 32768`; convert float16 to float32 before peak normalization and scaling. Preserve the existing mappings and silence handling.

This is not a full Gradio application/integration test or full repository suite.

Issue report only, in accordance with the current pause on external PRs. I checked existing issues/PRs: #7099/#7112 concern adding int8 support; #13396 concerns conversion for non-WAV outputs. This report concerns arithmetic inside the supported conversion branches.

cases.issue_title: `validator=` overwrites, and cannot reject, a `gr.State` in the event's `inputs=`
cases.issue_body:
### Describe the bug

Expected: `validator=` only decides whether the call proceeds — it shouldn't touch the value of any input, `gr.State` included.

Actual: attaching `validator=` to an event listener overwrites any `gr.State` in that event's `inputs=` with the validator's own return value, a dict like `{'__type__': 'validate', 'is_valid': ..., 'message': ...}`. Unlike other components, which get a fresh value from the client on their next call, `gr.State` has no such correction.

A `gr.State` input also can't be rejected: an invalid verdict never blocks the call, though the same validator blocks it correctly for a `Textbox`.

Not submitting a PR — `CONTRIBUTING.md` currently pauses outside PRs, so this is a report only.

### Have you searched existing issues?  🔎

- [x] I have searched and found no existing issues

### Reproduction

Both scripts launch the app in-process and drive it purely over HTTP via `gradio_client` — no browser needed.

### 1. The value is overwritten

Two triggers, same handler, same initial state value: one carries `validator=`, one (the control) doesn't. A third, validator-free trigger reads the same `gr.State` afterward, independent of the corrupting call.

```python
import gradio as gr
from gradio_client import Client


def handler(state_val):
    return repr(state_val)


def my_validator(state_val):
    return gr.validate(True, "")


with gr.Blocks() as demo:
    state = gr.State("genuine-value-42")
    out = gr.Textbox()
    with_validator_btn = gr.Button()
    with_validator_btn.click(
        fn=handler,
        inputs=[state],
        outputs=out,
        validator=my_validator,
        api_name="with_validator",
    )
    read_btn = gr.Button()
    read_btn.click(fn=handler, inputs=[state], outputs=out, api_name="read_after")

    control_state = gr.State("genuine-value-42")
    control_out = gr.Textbox()
    without_validator_btn = gr.Button()
    without_validator_btn.click(
        fn=handler,
        inputs=[control_state],
        outputs=control_out,
        api_name="without_validator",
    )


if __name__ == "__main__":
    demo.launch(prevent_thread_lock=True)
    client = Client(demo.local_url, verbose=False)
    expected = repr("genuine-value-42")

    with_validator = client.predict(api_name="/with_validator")
    read_after = client.predict(api_name="/read_after")
    without_validator = client.predict(api_name="/without_validator")

    print("with validator=, handler received:", with_validator)
    print("with validator=, state now holds:", read_after)
    print("without validator= (control):", without_validator)
    print(
        "PASS" if with_validator == expected and read_after == expected else "FAIL",
        "(with validator=)",
    )
    print("PASS" if without_validator == expected else "FAIL", "(control)")
    demo.close()
```

Output:

```
with validator=, handler received: {'__type__': 'validate', 'is_valid': True, 'message': ''}
with validator=, state now holds: {'__type__': 'validate', 'is_valid': True, 'message': ''}
without validator= (control): 'genuine-value-42'
FAIL (with validator=)
PASS (control)
```

Also reproduces with the `gr.State` in either input position (when there's more than one input), and with the validator returning all-valid or all-invalid.

### 2. An invalid verdict on the same `gr.State` input doesn't block the call

Same validator, two targets: a `gr.State` and, for contrast, an ordinary `Textbox`.

```python
import gradio as gr
from gradio_client import Client


def state_handler(state_val):
    return repr(state_val)


def invalid_state_validator(state_val):
    return gr.validate(False, "invalid")


def text_handler(text_val):
    return repr(text_val)


def invalid_text_validator(text_val):
    return gr.validate(False, "invalid")


with gr.Blocks() as demo:
    state = gr.State("genuine-value-42")
    state_btn = gr.Button()
    state_out = gr.Textbox()
    state_btn.click(
        fn=state_handler,
        inputs=[state],
        outputs=state_out,
        validator=invalid_state_validator,
    )

    tb = gr.Textbox(value="hello")
    text_btn = gr.Button()
    text_out = gr.Textbox()
    text_btn.click(
        fn=text_handler,
        inputs=[tb],
        outputs=text_out,
        validator=invalid_text_validator,
    )


if __name__ == "__main__":
    demo.launch(prevent_thread_lock=True)
    client = Client(demo.local_url, verbose=False)

    try:
        result = client.predict(api_name="/state_handler")
        print("gr.State input: handler ran ->", result, "(should have been rejected)")
    except Exception as e:
        print("gr.State input: rejected ->", e)

    try:
        result = client.predict("hello", api_name="/text_handler")
        print("Textbox input: handler ran ->", result, "(unexpected)")
    except Exception as e:
        print("Textbox input: rejected ->", e)

    demo.close()
```

Output:

```
gr.State input: handler ran -> {'__type__': 'validate', 'is_valid': False, 'message': 'invalid'} (should have been rejected)
Textbox input: rejected -> 1 parameter(s) failed validation:
- text_val: invalid
```

Expected: both rejected. `state_handler` ran instead — the exact same validator, targeting a `Textbox`, correctly rejects the call.

### Root cause (`gradio==6.25.0`) *— identified by Claude, not independently verified*

- `gradio/queueing.py`: when `fn.validator` is set, Gradio builds `validator_fn = BlockFunction(inputs=fn.inputs, outputs=fn.inputs, postprocess=False, ...)` — the validator's *outputs* are the real handler's *inputs*.
- `gradio/route_utils.py`: the validator call and the real call resolve the same `SessionState` (same `session_hash`).
- `gradio/blocks.py`, `process_api`: `postprocess_data` runs unconditionally after every `BlockFunction` call, including the validator's.
- `gradio/blocks.py`, `postprocess_data`'s `block.stateful` branch:
  ```python
  if block.stateful:
      prediction_value = predictions[i]
      if utils.is_prop_update(prediction_value):
          if "value" in prediction_value:
              state[block._id] = prediction_value["value"]
      else:
          state[block._id] = prediction_value
      output.append(None)
  ```
  Unlike the non-stateful branch just below it (`else:`, which itself branches on `block_fn.postprocess` via nested `elif` clauses), this branch ignores `block_fn.postprocess` entirely — so `postprocess=False` has no effect here.
- `gradio/utils.py`, `is_prop_update`: checks `"update" in val.get("__type__", "")`. `gr.validate()` returns `{"__type__": "validate", ...}`, which fails that check, so the `else` branch writes the raw dict straight into the `gr.State`.

Since `validator_fn.outputs == fn.inputs`, and validators are documented to return one `gr.validate()` per input, any `gr.State` among those inputs receives that per-input result as its new value — every call, valid or not.

This same `block.stateful` branch is also why the invalid verdict never reaches the client for a `gr.State` slot: it does `output.append(None)` unconditionally instead of returning the validate dict. `queueing.py`'s `process_validation_response` reads that `None` back from the response's `data` list, fails its `isinstance(data, dict)` check, and defaults to `{"is_valid": True, "message": ""}` for that slot — silently overriding whatever the validator actually returned. The sibling non-stateful branch has no equivalent short-circuit, which is why the same validator shape correctly rejects a `Textbox` input.

Both reproductions above were re-run against a fresh `gradio==6.27.0` install (current PyPI release) and produce identical output — this isn't fixed by upgrading.

### Narrower side effect: non-stateful inputs are also corrupted (dormant, exposed via `DeepLinkButton`)

The corrupting write isn't exclusive to `gr.State` — `postprocess_data`'s non-stateful path writes the same raw validate dict into `SessionState`'s tracked config value (`state._update_value_in_config`) for *every* input of the validated event, on every call, regardless of that input's own verdict. Normally this is invisible: the real handler runs right after and re-writes each input's correct value from the fresh request payload (`preprocess_data`), clobbering the validator's write before anything reads it back. But if *any* input is marked invalid, the real handler never runs at all — so none of the event's inputs get that self-healing write, and all of them stick with the corrupted dict, including inputs the validator itself marked valid.

This is dormant for ordinary interactive use (a live predict call always resupplies fresh values from the client, ignoring server-tracked config), but it does leak out through `gr.DeepLinkButton` ("Share via Link", auto-enabled on Hugging Face Spaces): its backend, `GET /gradio_api/deep_link`, snapshots exactly this tracked config and saves it as the state a shared link restores. A shared link generated after a rejected call corrupts every non-stateful input of that event this way, not just the one that failed validation — anyone who opens the link sees the raw `{'__type__': 'validate', ...}` dict instead of the real value. Confirmed this is the only consumer of that particular session data in the codebase (searched all references to `SessionState.config_values`/`.components`). Lower severity than the `gr.State` case — flagging for completeness since a fix should account for it too, not just the self-perpetuating `gr.State` symptom.

cases.issue_title: `ramping-arrival-rate` executor shows wrong progressbar
cases.issue_body:
### Brief summary

The [`ramping-arrival-rate` scenario executor](https://k6.io/docs/using-k6/scenarios/executors/ramping-arrival-rate/) doesn't handle situations in which the iteration rate doesn't match the duration exactly and iterations finish up very quickly. The progress bar appears unfinished and has a red cross (✗), suggesting that there was a problem, when in fact the executor finished normally.

### k6 version

any since k6 v0.27.0, i.e. this has been a problem since the initial introduction of the `ramping-arrival-rate` executor :sweat_smile:

### OS

Any

### Docker version and image (if applicable)

_No response_

### Steps to reproduce the problem

Have a script like this, where the iterations finish quickly and the scenario duration doesn't match the `timeUnit * iteration rate` exactly.
```js
export const options = {
    scenarios: {
        demo: {
            executor: 'ramping-arrival-rate',
            startRate: 1,
            preAllocatedVUs: 5,
            stages: [
                { duration: '2.5s', target: 1 },
            ],
        },
    },
};

export default function () {
    console.log(`iter`);
}

export function handleSummary(data) { }
```

### Expected behaviour

Expect the test run above to finish normally after running exactly 2 iterations.

### Actual behaviour

The test runs exactly 2 iterations, but the progress bar makes it seem like the scenario didn't fully finish or there and was instead prematurely interrupted:
```
...
INFO[0001] iter                                          source=console
INFO[0002] iter                                          source=console

running (02.0s), 0/1 VUs, 2 complete and 0 interrupted iterations
demo ✗ [=============================>--------] 0/1 VUs  2.0s/2.5s  1.00 iters/s
...
```

Basically, it seems like the executor just aborts early, since it has finished all of the 2 iterations it was supposed to execute and it "knows" it's not going to have time to start that third iteration. That is normal and good and desired. However, it doesn't seem to update its progressbar correctly :disappointed: 

One way to "fix" the progress bars is to force the executor it to wait, i.e. slow down the iterations. If I just add `sleep(2)` in the iteration, and then the progress bar is displayed correctly. But so far this seems like just a visualization issue, the execution seems to be working as expected :relieved:

cases.issue_title: Duration metric is not accurate for "double TLS" MITM proxies (edge case)
cases.issue_body: ### Brief summary I'm writing this up to document an edge case where K6 http request duration metrics are not accurate. This isn't something that will affect many people, but it's here mostly for Google or anyone stumbling upon it. I have been using K6 to test a MITM proxy that is called via TLS, and then talks upstream via TLS. Consider an application that receives an environment variable `HTTPS_PROXY=https://foo...`. There are two TLS handshakes here: between the client and proxy, and between the client and upstream. The problem is this breaks assumptions made by K6's metrics: - `blocked` covers the period from `getConn` to `gotConn`. It includes both TLS handshakes. - `duration` covers the period from the _first_ TLSHandshakeDone to the end of the request The issue is, because there are two TLS Handshakes, this means the `blocked` period and `duration` overlap. This inflates the assumed overall time of the request, because instead of duration strictly being `sending + waiting + receiving`, it includes the second TLS step as well In other words, the second TLS negotiation is effectively counted twice in the metrics This is a fairly unusual setup and ultimately this isn't going to be a problem for my tests. However I think it's worth flagging up in case anyone is seeing a TLS double-count or mismatching values with a MITM SSL proxy. The actual solution might be as simple as to only count `duration` as starting from `GotConn` ### k6 version 1.8.1 ### OS Ubuntu 26.04 ### Docker version and image (if applicable) _No response_ ### Steps to reproduce the problem - Run K6 with HTTPS_PROXY env var set to a https-transport based proxy - Make connections with no connection reuse (TLS renegotiation each time) - Observe how duration + blocked is larger than total time of request to complete ### Expected behaviour - Blocked + duration should cover the whole request time ### Actual behaviour - Second TLS negotiation time is double-counted

### Brief summary

`digestTransport.RoundTrip` does not close the initial 401 response body when reading the digest challenge body fails.

Current master

All platforms (reproduced on macOS 26.5.2)

Not applicable

4. Inspect the response body after the read error is returned.

cases.issue_title: URL parsing of --out influxdb= not optimal
cases.issue_body:
First off, thanks for a great piece of awesome-sauce. So far I love working with k6!

Now to what is causing me some headache. I have several InfluxDBs hosted behind a reverse proxy that uses paths to send traffic to the correct InfluxDB instance. However, the behaviour of `--out influxdb` only allows me to specify the hostname, and not the sub-path of the InfluxDB instance. k6 automatically interprets the path-portion of the URL to be the InfluxDB database. So using `https://my.site.io/influxdbA/k6db` results in k6 trying to connect to InfluxDB hosted on `my.site.io` and using database `influxdbA/k6db`. Instead of my intended behaviour of connecting to `https://my.site.io/influxdbA/` and use database `k6db`.

Here is a few suggestions:
  - Only the last portion of the URL should be interpreted as the database name. Will be a problem if people are using database names with `/`, even though I'm not sure if that is allowed in InfluxDB.
  - Specify the database as an argument, like `site.io/influxA?db=k6db`.
  - Specify the database as a separate argument from the InfluxDB URL itself.

cases.issue_title: GaugeSink reports max = 0 when all gauge samples are negative (missing maxSet guard in metrics/sink.go)
cases.issue_body:
**VERIFIED:** 2026-07-20, built from master `99d25c36` on darwin/arm64; ran the JS repro and a Go unit test against the real `metrics` package. v2.1.0 tag carries the same code at the same lines.

---

## Title

`GaugeSink` reports `max = 0` when all gauge samples are negative (missing `maxSet` guard in `metrics/sink.go`)

---

## Brief summary

`GaugeSink.Add` compares each sample against the zero-initialized `Max` field with a plain `s.Value > g.Max` check. `Min` gets a first-sample guard (`|| !g.minSet`); `Max` gets none. A gauge whose samples are all negative therefore reports `max = 0` in the end-of-test summary and in every summary/JSON export that includes gauge min/max, even though no sample ever had that value.

Root cause (`metrics/sink.go` lines 91–99, identical on current master `99d25c36` and on the v2.1.0 tag):

```go
func (g *GaugeSink) Add(s Sample) {
	g.Value = s.Value
	if s.Value > g.Max {          // <-- no maxSet guard: Max stays 0 for all-negative series
		g.Max = s.Value
	}
	if s.Value < g.Min || !g.minSet {  // <-- Min DOES have the first-sample guard
		g.Min = s.Value
		g.minSet = true
	}
}
```

Both summary paths read `sink.Max` for gauges (`internal/js/summary.go:109-112` and `internal/output/summary/data.go:403-406`), so the wrong value reaches users directly.

Suggested fix: reuse the existing `minSet` flag as the first-sample guard for `Max`. `Add` checks it before setting it, so no new field is needed:

```go
	if s.Value > g.Max || !g.minSet {
		g.Max = s.Value
	}
```

(Or add a symmetric `maxSet bool`.) `Min` already has the guard, so positive-only gauges keep their current behavior; the bug bites only for negative values, which `Gauge` supports.

## k6 version

v2.1.0 (latest release). Also present on current `master`: built `99d25c36` locally (`k6 v2.1.1-0.20260720081940-99d25c36859b`) and reproduced there.

## OS

macOS (darwin/arm64). Platform-independent.

## Docker version and image (if applicable)

n/a

## Steps to reproduce the problem

`repro.js`:

```js
import { Gauge } from 'k6/metrics';

const depth = new Gauge('queue_depth_delta'); // a metric that can go negative

export default function () {
  depth.add(-5);
  depth.add(-3);
  depth.add(-8);
}
```

Run:

```sh
k6 run --iterations 1 --vus 1 repro.js
```

and read the `queue_depth_delta` line in the end-of-test summary (or `handleSummary` data / `--summary-export`).

Pure-Go reproduction of the sink itself:

```go
g := metrics.GaugeSink{}
for _, v := range []float64{-5, -3, -8} {
	g.Add(metrics.Sample{Value: v})
}
fmt.Println(g.Min, g.Max) // prints: -8 0   (want: -8 -3)
```

## Expected behaviour

`max` is the largest observed sample, `-3`:

```
queue_depth_delta....: -8  min=-8       max=-3
```

## Actual behaviour

`max` is `0`, a value never added to the gauge. Output from the master build:

```
    CUSTOM
    queue_depth_delta....: -8  min=-8       max=0
```

`--summary-export` gives the same: `{"value": -8, "min": -8, "max": 0}`.

`min` and `value` are correct. `max` goes wrong when every sample is `< 0`; a single sample `>= 0` masks the bug. Any all-negative gauge (queue-depth deltas, temperature-style metrics, error budgets) gets a misleading `max` in the end-of-test summary, `handleSummary`, and `--summary-export`.

---

*If this is intended / by-design: I'm really sorry, please just close it — no need to flag or ban me. I'm trying to scale property-based testing across the whole ecosystem and my publishing agents may have gotten this one wrong. I read every issue and follow up on each.*

cases.issue_title: test-xk6: flaky failures on Linux/macOS runners due to Go module proxy race for fork commits
cases.issue_body:
# test-xk6: flaky failures on Linux/macOS runners due to Go module proxy race for fork commits

## Summary

The `test-xk6` workflow intermittently fails on Linux and macOS runners when triggered by a pull request from a **fork**. Re-running the exact same failed jobs a few minutes later makes them pass without any code change. The root cause is a timing race between the CI runners and `proxy.golang.org` populating a brand-new pseudo-version.

## Observed behavior

In run [29948532385](https://github.com/grafana/k6/actions/runs/29948532385), triggered by a fork PR (head sha `750f556b`), the matrix produced this split:

| Job | Result |
|-----|--------|
| `test-xk6 (stable, ubuntu-latest)` | ❌ failure |
| `test-xk6 (stable, ubuntu-24.04-arm)` | ❌ failure |
| `test-xk6 (tip, ubuntu-latest)` | ❌ failure |
| `test-xk6 (tip, ubuntu-24.04-arm)` | ❌ failure |
| `test-xk6 (stable, macos-latest)` | ❌ failure |
| `test-xk6 (tip, macos-latest)` | ✅ success |
| `test-xk6 (stable, windows-latest)` | ✅ success |
| `test-xk6 (tip, windows-latest)` | ✅ success |

All failing jobs errored at the `xk6 build` step:

```
INF adding dependency go.k6.io/k6/v2 => github.com/the-onewho-knocks/k6/v2@750f556b9ccb3074959ed788edd1a81d8436fead
INF Cleaning up work directory /tmp/k6foundry...
ERR resolving dependency: executing go command: exit status 1
##[error]Process completed with exit code 1.
```

After re-running the failed jobs ~1 hour later (no code change, same commit), **all jobs passed**. This confirms the failure is not caused by any defect in the PR code.

## Root cause

### How the workflow resolves fork commits

When a PR comes from a fork, [xk6.yml](https://github.com/grafana/k6/blob/master/.github/workflows/xk6.yml) detects that `github.event.pull_request.head.repo.full_name != github.repository` and sets:

```bash
export XK6_K6_REPO="github.com/${PR_REPO}"
```

xk6/k6foundry then adds a Go module replace directive:

```
go.k6.io/k6/v2 => github.com/<fork-owner>/k6/v2 @ <head-sha>
```

Because `GOPRIVATE` is set to `go.k6.io/k6` only — and **not** to `github.com/<fork-owner>/k6` — Go resolves the replacement module through the **public `proxy.golang.org` and `sum.golang.org`** rather than fetching directly from GitHub.

### The race

When a commit is freshly pushed to a fork, `proxy.golang.org` has not yet fetched and published the corresponding pseudo-version. The first request to the proxy triggers a background fetch (cloning the fork, building the module zip, submitting hashes to `sum.golang.org`). This process can take **1–2 minutes** for a large repo like k6.

During that window, concurrent Go client requests for the same pseudo-version receive a transient error from the proxy (exit status 1). The underlying Go error is swallowed by xk6/k6foundry, which surfaces only the generic `ERR resolving dependency: executing go command: exit status 1`.

### Why the platform split is consistent

The failing jobs (Linux x64, Linux arm64, stable macOS) started at **19:03:40Z** and failed fast — all completing by **19:05:27Z**, roughly 1.5 minutes in. This is exactly when `xk6 build` ran the `go` resolution step.

The passing jobs (Windows x64/arm, tip macOS) spent more time on setup (downloading and unzipping the Go tip toolchain, slower provisioning) before reaching the same `go` resolution step — by which point the proxy had finished populating the module.

The proxy's own record confirms the timeline:

```json
{
  "Version": "v2.0.0-20260722185143-750f556b9ccb",
  "Time": "2026-07-22T18:51:43Z"
}
```

The commit was pushed at **18:51:43Z**. The workflow started at **19:03:40Z** — 12 minutes later. The proxy had *started* the fetch but had not yet completed it when the fast Linux runners requested the module.

After the proxy fully populated the entry (visible in `sum.golang.org` having the `h1:` hash), re-running the failed jobs succeeded immediately — with a completely cold module cache, the resolution now works without any retries.

## Impact

This race affects **every fork PR** on every push. It is not limited to this specific PR or contributor. Because the window is short, it manifests as a flaky failure that developers typically work around by re-running CI, without realizing the underlying structural cause.

## Proposed fix

The fix is to make Go resolve the fork module directly from GitHub (bypassing the proxy population race and the checksum database) by extending `GOPRIVATE` to include the fork's GitHub path. In the `Run tests` step of `xk6.yml`, when `XK6_K6_REPO` is set, also export:

```bash
if [ "${{ github.event_name }}" == "pull_request" -a \
     "${PR_REPO}" != "${{ github.repository }}" ]; then
  export XK6_K6_REPO="github.com/${PR_REPO}"
  export GOPRIVATE="go.k6.io/k6,github.com/${PR_REPO}"  # <-- add this
fi
```

With the fork in `GOPRIVATE`, the `go` toolchain fetches it directly via git and skips `proxy.golang.org` and `sum.golang.org` entirely. This eliminates the race: there is no proxy to populate, so the module is always immediately available regardless of how quickly the runner reaches that step.

A secondary improvement would be to add `GONOSUMDB` or `GONOSUMCHECK` coverage for the fork path as a belt-and-suspenders measure, though `GOPRIVATE` already implies both `GONOPROXY` and `GONOSUMDB`.
